title: Adaptive Cadence Slots: Pre-commit Buffer and Scope Arbitration Protocol
creator: Priya Desai
description: Background: As Redwood scales Dedicated and Private signups, product teams repeatedly hit mid-cycle churn where high-priority incidents and new sales commitments displace planned deliverables. Current cycle buffer rules are ad hoc and often lead to rushed scope cuts or late shipping features. Goal: Define an operational protocol (Adaptive Cadence Slots) that formalizes a pre-commit buffer, a predictable swap process for critical staff reassignments, and a lightweight arbitration flow for scope reductions so PMs and Eng leads can make timely, low-regret decisions. Outcomes: 1) Reduced mid-cycle churn and better predictability for dependent teams; 2) Clear ownership and SLAs for surge reassignments; 3) A documented runbook that integrates with CycleOps tooling and weekly capacity snapshots.
acceptance_criteria: Runbook published in Confluence with decision trees and SLA targets
CycleOps dashboard shows buffer headroom and active slot assignments for the next 4 weeks
Triaged scope-cut template and two example rollups validated with Eng and Design
Pilot applied in 2026-W13 across two cross-functional initiatives with post-mortem metrics
decisions: Buffer size set to 12% of committed velocity for medium cycles, adjustable by exec approval
Two-tier reassign policy: Tier A (<=3 days) can be enacted by Eng PMs; Tier B (>3 days) requires triage board approval
Scope arbitration will prefer de-scoping non-customer-impacting backend tasks before user-visible features

postmortem_metrics: % of scope delivered vs committed (pilot goal >= 85%)
number of mid-cycle reassignments resolved within SLA (target >= 90%)
time to decision for scope arbitration (target <= 48 hours)
qualitative stakeholder satisfaction score (post-pilot survey goal >= 4/5)
open_questions: Should buffer policy differ for Dedicated vs Hosted product tracks?
What authority level should be required to cancel an active slot if a customer escalates?
How do we prevent buffer gaming by artificially deferring tasks into the buffer?
